name: Sîn-lēqi-unninni and the Standard Babylonian version of the Epic of Gilgamesh (Akkadian incipit 'Sha naqba īmuru', 'He Who Saw the Deep')
date: Editorial work placed in the late second millennium BC: 'probably in the period between 1300 BC and 1000 BC' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%AEn-l%C4%93qi-unninni); Tigay puts it in the Middle Babylonian period, 'some time in the last half or quarter of the second millennium' (Tigay, The Evolution of the Gilgamesh Epic, 1982, https://epdf.pub/the-evolution-of-the-gilgamesh-epic.html). The date is a scholarly inference, not a record. The version was 'current in the eighth to second centuries BCE' (BMCR 2004.04.21, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.21/). Key surviving copies are 7th-century BC tablets from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh; the Flood tablet K.3375 was found by Hormuzd Rassam in 1853 and George Smith presented his reading of it on 3 December 1872 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh_flood_myth, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Smith_(Assyriologist)). The authorship attribution comes from W. G. Lambert, 'A Catalogue of Texts and Authors', Journal of Cuneiform Studies 16 (1962) (cited in Helle 2018, https://sophushelle.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/helle-2018-role-of-authors.pdf)
creator: Sîn-lēqi-unninni ('Sîn (the Moon God) is one who accepts my prayer'), a mašmaššu, i.e. exorcist-priest, of Uruk (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%AEn-l%C4%93qi-unninni; Tigay 1982: 'Mesopotamian tradition credited this epic to an exorcist-priest named Sîn-leqi-unninnī'). Known only through later tradition. The Neo-Assyrian Catalogue of Texts and Authors credits the Epic of Gilgamesh to him (Lambert 1962; Helle 2018), and 'his name appears in a catalogue of texts and authors, not on any tablet of the poem itself' (Michael Schmidt, Literary Hub, https://lithub.com/who-were-the-scribes-who-actually-wrote-down-the-epic-of-gilgamesh/). The Uruk List of Kings and Sages, copied at Uruk on 16 May 165 BC by the lamentation priest Anu-belshunu, reads in Helle's translation: '[In the time of] king? [Gilgam]esh?: the scholar was Sin-leqi-unninni.' The copyist signs as 'descendant of Sin-leqi-unnenni' (Helle 2018). Modern reconstruction of the text is chiefly by Andrew George (The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003) and, since 2018, the Electronic Babylonian Library team at LMU Munich led by Enrique Jiménez (https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091)
form: Cuneiform clay tablets in Standard Babylonian Akkadian: an edited recension of older Old Babylonian material, which 'runs to some three thousand lines, split into twelve standard "Tablets" or chapters' (BMCR 2004.04.21, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.21/). Tablets I to XI form the epic proper; Tablet XII renders the Sumerian 'Gilgamesh, Enkidu, and the Netherworld' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%AEn-l%C4%93qi-unninni) and 'was probably appended at a later date' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh). About two-thirds of the twelve-tablet version has been recovered (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh). The 'version' is a text reconstructed from many manuscripts, not a single physical object
effect_on_arc: Comparing the recensions shows the Standard version reframed the story. The Old Babylonian version was titled after its incipit 'Shūtur eli sharrī' ('Surpassing All Other Kings'); the Standard version opens 'Sha naqba īmuru' ('He Who Saw the Deep(s)') (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh). Tigay (1982) notes that the Old Babylonian hymn 'Surpassing the rulers, renowned...' 'formed the introduction to the Old Babylonian version', while the new prologue virtually ignores heroic deeds and instead 'mentions the outcome of Gilgamesh's quest, the understanding that he gained', stressing the verbs 'see' and 'know'. The prologue tells the reader to open a tablet box and 'read aloud from the lapis-lazuli tablet [How/that] Gilgamesh went through all hardships' (Tigay's translation, I 22-26), and its walls-of-Uruk passage is repeated at the end of Tablet XI ('XI, 303-7 = I, i, 16-21'), framing the poem as a ring that ends on the city rather than the lost plant (https://epdf.pub/the-evolution-of-the-gilgamesh-epic.html). Utnapishtim's Flood story sits in Tablet XI (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%AEn-l%C4%93qi-unninni). Siduri's Old Babylonian advice to accept death and enjoy life 'is absent' from the Standard version, where she only directs Gilgamesh to the boatman Urshanabi (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siduri). How much of this is Sîn-lēqi-unninni's own work is not settled: Tigay says 'the prologue and Tablet XII were first added in this version or earlier, at some intermediate stage', and that his achievement was 'some important Middle Babylonian version' rather than the original. The net effect is a wisdom epic about mortality and the limits of kingship, where the older poem opened as praise of a heroic king
critical_response: Assyriologists treat Sîn-lēqi-unninni as the nearest thing the epic has to an author, with caution. Lambert's 1962 catalogue publication established the attribution. Tigay (1982) 'helped establish the notion that the standard "late version" of the epic was in ways an original work of art itself, rather than a collection of earlier anecdotes' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_H._Tigay), while concluding that his contribution was a Middle Babylonian version, not the first one (https://epdf.pub/the-evolution-of-the-gilgamesh-epic.html). Andrew George argues he 'gave [The Epic of Gilgamesh] its final, fixed form' (quoted at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%AEn-l%C4%93qi-unninni). Michael Schmidt describes the contribution as curatorial, organising scattered Old Babylonian stories into one narrative (https://lithub.com/who-were-the-scribes-who-actually-wrote-down-the-epic-of-gilgamesh/). Sophus Helle (2018) reads the late interest in named authors as a first-millennium development, 'as cuneiform culture waned, the figure of the author waxed', with authors invoked 'as mythical family ancestors' (https://sophushelle.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/helle-2018-role-of-authors.pdf)
controversies: (1) Author or editor: whether he composed new poetry or compiled and revised older material; Tigay and Schmidt lean to editor or curator, George credits him with the fixed form. (2) Historicity: all evidence is centuries later, and Wikipedia notes 'He may have been a legendary figure', later described as 'Gilgamesh's wise councilor' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%AEn-l%C4%93qi-unninni). (3) Scope: Tigay cannot say whether the prologue and Tablet XII were added by him or at an intermediate stage. (4) Dating rests on indirect evidence (1300 to 1000 BC is an estimate). (5) A factual error in circulation: Wikipedia says 'His name is listed in the text itself', but Schmidt states his name appears 'in a catalogue of texts and authors, not on any tablet of the poem itself' (https://lithub.com/who-were-the-scribes-who-actually-wrote-down-the-epic-of-gilgamesh/)
regional_reception: The Standard version is tied to Uruk (modern Warka, southern Iraq). The Uruk List of Kings and Sages that pairs him with Gilgamesh is held in the Baghdad Museum (Helle 2018, https://sophushelle.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/helle-2018-role-of-authors.pdf). The Iraqi archaeologist Taha Baqir published the first direct Arabic translation from the cuneiform in 1962, reprinted in more than six editions and still sold on Baghdad's Al-Mutanabi Street (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taha_Baqir, https://medium.com/@ahmedwindi94/the-clay-reader-b6ec0f6e0e17) [uncertain: whether Arabic editions foreground Sîn-lēqi-unninni by name]. The Nineveh manuscripts, including the Flood tablet, remain in the British Museum in London
method: Cuneiform scholarship and textual criticism: decipherment of the Nineveh tablets (George Smith, 1872), joins of fragments across collections, and collation of manuscripts into a critical edition (George 2003, from 184 fragments, 'some 25 of which are completely new to this edition', BMCR 2004.04.21, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.21/). Comparison of Old, Middle and Standard Babylonian recensions isolates the editorial layer (Tigay 1982). The attribution rests on reading ancient catalogues (Lambert 1962) and the Uruk List of Kings and Sages (first published by Jan van Dijk, 1962). Photo-based identification of stray fragments continued (Jiménez, 'New Fragments of Gilgameš and Other Literary Texts from Kuyunjik', Iraq 76, 2014, three new Gilgamesh fragments found via the British Museum's online photographs, https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/49550/1/Jimenez_New_Fragments_of_Gilgames_and_other_Literary_Texts_from_Kuyunjik.pdf). Since 2018 the Electronic Babylonian Library has added computational string alignment against its digitised Fragmentarium
ai_pipeline_stage: Fragment matching. The eBL uses a 'string alignment algorithm specifically tailored for cuneiform' on transliterated fragments to find pieces that belong together; this is not machine learning. The project's separate AI work concerns disambiguating cuneiform sign readings (https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091). Human Assyriologists verify each match. Deciding what belongs to Sîn-lēqi-unninni's edition remains entirely human
scale_metrics: George 2003: 184 fragments, against 108 available to Campbell Thompson (BMCR 2004.04.21, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.21/). Standard version: about 3,000 lines in twelve tablets (same source); about two-thirds recovered (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh). eBL: before 2018 about 5,000 tablet fragments had been matched; in six years the team matched over 1,500 more, 'including 20 fragments from Gilgamesh that add detail to over 100 lines of the epic' (New York Times, Erik Ofgang, 12 August 2024, as quoted at https://paleojudaica.blogspot.com/2024/08/ai-is-finding-more-gilgamesh-epic.html?m=1). One Nineveh manuscript of the prologue, K.4981+, was rebuilt 'from nine discrete fragments previously transliterated in the Fragmentarium' (https://theconversation.com/ai-is-helping-us-read-ancient-mesopotamian-literature-205091). Manuscript dates: 7th century BC (Nineveh) to the 2nd century BC; the edit itself is dated about 1300 to 1000 BC
what_was_found: Not a single object but an identity and an edition: the name of the epic's editor, recovered from the Catalogue of Texts and Authors (Lambert 1962) and the Uruk List of Kings and Sages (van Dijk 1962; Helle 2018), and the reconstructed Standard Babylonian text, with its knowledge-centred prologue 'He Who Saw the Deep', the ring structure closing on the walls of Uruk, the Flood story in Tablet XI and the appended Tablet XII. This recension is the spine most modern English translations follow
provenance_and_ethics: The Nineveh manuscripts were excavated for the British Museum in the mid-19th century under Ottoman rule; the Flood tablet K.3375 was found by Hormuzd Rassam in 1853 on a mission for Austen Henry Layard (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh_flood_myth) and remains in London. That was lawful at the time but belongs to the wider debate over colonial-era removal of Iraqi heritage. The Uruk List of Kings and Sages (excavation number W 20030,7) came from German excavations at Uruk and is in the Baghdad Museum (Helle 2018, https://sophushelle.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/helle-2018-role-of-authors.pdf). The British Museum's online photographs made the Kuyunjik collection searchable worldwide (Jiménez 2014), and the eBL Fragmentarium publishes transliterations openly, with more than 22,000 fragments digitised by 2023 (https://paleojudaica.blogspot.com/2024/08/ai-is-finding-more-gilgamesh-epic.html?m=1)
ai_craft_tension: Sîn-lēqi-unninni is the first person we can name who did what every later translator does: took an inherited Gilgamesh, cut, added and reordered it, and gave it a new frame. Machines now help rebuild his text. The eBL's alignment software finds pieces that belong to it faster than a scholar reading museum drawers could; 20 fragments and more than 100 lines since 2018. But the software recovers words, not choices. Deciding that a line belongs to his edition and not to an earlier layer (a question Tigay could not settle for the prologue), seeing that the prologue and the close of Tablet XI mirror each other, and reading that as a shift from heroic boast to wisdom about death, all take a human literary reader. There is a neat loop too: the ancient 'author' was himself a compiler working from sources, so the question AI now raises about authorship (is assembling prior text creative?) was already being asked of him. The epic's answer seems to be yes, if the assembler has a point of view
essay_hooks: (1) A list copied at Uruk in 165 BC names him as Gilgamesh's own scholar: '[In the time of] king? [Gilgam]esh?: the scholar was Sin-leqi-unninni.' The copyist, Anu-belshunu, signed as his 'descendant' (Helle 2018, https://sophushelle.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/helle-2018-role-of-authors.pdf). An editor promoted into the story he edited. (2) His name means 'Sîn (the Moon God) is one who accepts my prayer', and his job was exorcist (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%AEn-l%C4%93qi-unninni). (3) The opening changed from 'Surpassing All Other Kings' to 'He Who Saw the Deep(s)' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh): Tigay notes the new prologue stresses 'see' and 'know', 'wisdom' and 'secret(s)'. (4) The prologue tells you to open a box and 'read aloud from the lapis-lazuli tablet' (Tigay's translation): the poem announces that it is a written document. (5) Siduri's famous enjoy-life speech is absent from the Standard version (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siduri), so some of the most quoted lines of 'Gilgamesh' are not in the text most people think they are reading. (6) His name appears 'in a catalogue of texts and authors, not on any tablet of the poem itself' (Schmidt, https://lithub.com/who-were-the-scribes-who-actually-wrote-down-the-epic-of-gilgamesh/). (7) The eBL's algorithm has added 20 Gilgamesh fragments and detail to over 100 lines since 2018 (NYT, 12 August 2024, via https://paleojudaica.blogspot.com/2024/08/ai-is-finding-more-gilgamesh-epic.html?m=1): the latest step in a chain of editors that begins with him
